summary: An April 1st joke RFC that reformulates IP, TCP and UDP as XML applications under the name Binary Lexical Octet Ad-hoc Transport. It is humor, not a real protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC pretends to replace compact network packets with verbose XML documents. It defines the joke format in detail, including XML layouts and ways to carry the data.

questions: what is binary lexical octet ad-hoc transport
subtitle: An April 1st RFC that rewrites IP, TCP, and UDP packets as XML documents.

tldr.problem: The joke premise is that XML's use in application protocols should be extended to network and transport protocols too.
tldr.mechanism: BLOAT describes XML forms for IPv4, TCP, and UDP, encodes payloads in Base64, and specifies Ethernet and IEEE 802 transport details.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3252 is an April 1st joke, not a real protocol deployment. It says the underlying protocol behavior remains unchanged while the encoding becomes XML.

today: RFC 3252 is an April 1st Informational joke. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The BLOAT Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 3252 is an April 1st joke describing Binary Lexical Octet Ad-hoc Transport (BLOAT). It reformulates IP, TCP, and UDP as XML applications and describes carrying BLOAT over Ethernet and IEEE 802 networks, or encapsulating it in IP.

The RFC's stated motivation is that XML is used in application protocols, so a single XML parser might handle more of the protocol stack. It says the behavior of routing, address spaces, and TCP congestion control remains as specified in the existing protocols; only the encoding changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC jokes about using XML for network and transport layers as well as applications. It claims that the packet behavior stays the same even though every field becomes XML.

sections.title: IPoXML, TCPoXML, and UDPoXML
sections.content:
The memo defines document forms for IP, TCP, and UDP, with separate DTDs. Values such as bit masks become readable attributes, and address, length, checksum, and port values are written as text. Implementations MUST use UTF-8 and well-formed documents with an XML declaration.

Because an IP payload may contain arbitrary data, the RFC requires Base64 encoding. Length and checksum calculations use a canonicalized XML form. TCP and UDP documents inside IPoXML may omit the XML declaration and DOCTYPE. The RFC supplies sample datagrams and notes that XML expands the headers substantially.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol becomes a structured XML document with named fields. Payload bytes are represented as Base64 text so they can fit in XML.

sections.title: Transport and Gatewaying
sections.content:
For Ethernet, the RFC specifies an Ethernet type value of 0xBEEF; the first five octets of the payload spell <?xml. For IEEE 802 networks, it also assigns 0xBEEF as the IPoXML protocol type code.

BLOAT may be encapsulated in IP to connect networks using BLOAT on their LANs. The document includes DTDs for the network and transport documents and notes that implementations would normally embed the DTD rather than fetch it over the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke format uses a distinctive Ethernet value and can be carried inside ordinary IP for gatewaying. Its XML document rules are defined by DTDs.
